I Prehistory

Scotland Before Scotland

Before there was a Scotland, there was a hard northern landscape of islands, mountains, glens, river valleys, fortified hills, and coastal kingdoms. Geography mattered from the very beginning. Scotland was never one easy-to-rule plain. It was a broken country: the Highlands, the Lowlands, the Islands, the Borders, the northeast, each with its own pressures, languages, loyalties, and political instincts.

That is one reason Scottish history often feels less like a single royal chronicle and more like a shifting board of rival houses, sacred places, warrior elites, religious reformers, ambitious queens, suspicious nobles, and foreign kings.

The people who eventually formed Scotland were not one original ethnic group. The kingdom emerged from layers of peoples: Picts, Gaels (whom the Romans called Scotti), Britons, Angles, Norse settlers, and later Norman-influenced aristocrats. Scotland was made, not simply born.

The very oldest layers of human life in this land are visible at sites like Skara Brae on Orkney, a Neolithic village preserved by sand for nearly five thousand years. A reminder, before any of the kings and queens, that this place had been inhabited and shaped for an almost unimaginable span of time.

Stop and think
Why does it matter for understanding Scottish history that the country was 'made, not simply born'? What political consequences flow from that fact?
Quick check
Which of the following peoples was NOT among the early layers that shaped Scotland?
The Visigoths were a Germanic people who moved into the western Roman Empire (Spain, southern Gaul). Scotland was shaped by Picts, Gaels, Britons, Angles, Norse, and later Norman-influenced families.
II Roman Frontier

Rome and the Northern Frontier

Rome conquered much of Britain, but northern Britain was never absorbed in the same way as the south. Roman armies campaigned into what is now Scotland, and the empire built frontier systems, especially Hadrian's Wall starting in AD 122, and later the Antonine Wall starting in AD 142. But Rome's grip was temporary.

This mattered psychologically and politically for centuries to come. Scotland's identity often drew power from the idea of being the place Rome could not finally hold. That story is partly mythic, because Rome did influence southern Scotland and interacted with local societies. But it is not empty myth. The north remained a frontier, not a fully Roman province.

The people Rome called Picts became one of the major forces in early medieval northern Britain. The name probably comes from Roman descriptions of 'painted' or marked people, though the exact meaning and identity of the Picts remain debated even today.

Stop and think
If Rome had successfully conquered and held all of what is now Scotland, how might Scottish identity have developed differently?
Quick check
Which wall was built FIRST?
Hadrian's Wall was begun in AD 122. The Antonine Wall came later, beginning in AD 142.
III Early Medieval

Picts, Gaels, Vikings, and the Kingdom of Alba

After Rome withdrew from Britain, power fragmented. Northern Britain became a world of competing kingdoms. The major forces were the Picts, dominant across eastern and northern Scotland; the Gaels or Scots, associated with Dál Riata in the west; the Britons in the south and southwest; the Angles expanding north out of Northumbria; and the Norse who from the late 8th century onward reshaped Orkney, Shetland, Caithness, the Hebrides, and large stretches of the coast.

Christianity became one of the great unifying forces. Iona, associated with St Columba, who founded the monastery there in 563, became a major spiritual and intellectual center. Monasteries were not merely religious buildings. They were archives, diplomatic centers, schools, memory machines, and political actors.

The later kingdom of Alba emerged from this violent mixture. Traditional history gives a central role to Kenneth MacAlpin, often described as uniting Picts and Scots around 843. Modern historians are more cautious. It was likely not a single heroic unification, but a longer process of dynastic consolidation, warfare, and elite marriage.

By the early medieval period, something recognizably Scottish was forming. But it was still fragile, and the Viking presence would not begin to fade for centuries.

Stop and think
How is the role of Iona different from the role of, say, a royal castle? What did monasteries do politically, beyond serving religion?
Quick check
What was Dál Riata?
Dál Riata was a Gaelic kingdom that bridged western Scotland (Argyll) and northeastern Ireland. It was the seedbed of Gaelic culture in Scotland.
IV Davidian Era

Medieval Kingship: Scotland Becomes a Kingdom

Medieval Scotland became more organized under kings who extended royal authority, founded towns, promoted monasteries, and invited continental legal and feudal ideas.

A major figure here is David I, king from 1124 to 1153. His reign helped transform Scotland through what historians sometimes call the Davidian Revolution. This included Burghs, chartered towns that encouraged trade; feudal lordship tying landholding to service and loyalty; monastic foundations that strengthened royal power; and the integration of Anglo-Norman aristocratic families into the Scottish elite.

This was not cultural replacement. It was layering. Gaelic kingship did not vanish overnight. The Highlands and western regions retained older kinship-based systems. The Lowlands became more integrated with European feudal and commercial life.

This split between Gaelic Highlands culture and Scots-speaking Lowlands culture would become one of the most consequential divisions in Scottish history, with consequences reaching all the way to Culloden in 1746 and beyond.

Stop and think
Why is 'layering' a better description of medieval Scottish cultural change than 'replacement'? What does that imply about cultural change in general?
Quick check
Which of these is a chartered medieval Scottish town with royal trading privileges?
Burghs were chartered towns granted special trading and legal privileges by the crown. They were central to David I's economic and political reforms.
V Wars of Independence

The Wars of Independence

The late 13th and early 14th centuries were decisive. When Alexander III died in 1286, Scotland faced a succession crisis. His heir, Margaret, Maid of Norway, died in 1290 before she could take the throne. That left rival claimants competing for power. Into this crisis stepped Edward I of England, who attempted to dominate Scotland politically. This was the moment Scotland's independence became a battlefield question.

William Wallace rose as a resistance leader and became famous after the Scottish victory at Stirling Bridge in 1297. Wallace was later captured, taken to London, and executed in 1305. His death made him useful to memory: the betrayed patriot, the rebel martyr, the man whose body could be destroyed but whose cause could not.

But the more politically successful figure was Robert the Bruce. Bruce's path was morally and politically complicated. He was not a pure folk hero from the beginning. He was a nobleman navigating claims, alliances, betrayals, and brutal necessity. His killing of John Comyn in 1306 at Greyfriars was a shocking act that helped clear his path to the throne but also stained his legitimacy.

Bruce's great victory came at Bannockburn in 1314. It did not instantly settle everything, but it became one of the defining symbolic victories in Scottish history.

Stop and think
Wallace and Bruce occupy different roles in Scottish memory. Why might a martyr be 'useful' to a national cause in ways a successful king is not?
Quick check
Which event happened FIRST?
Stirling Bridge (1297) came before Wallace's execution (1305), Bruce killing Comyn (1306), and Bannockburn (1314).
VI Arbroath

The Declaration of Arbroath

The Declaration of Arbroath in 1320 gave ideological force to the cause. It declared Scotland's independence and presented kingship as conditional: the king existed to defend the realm. This was not democracy in the modern sense. It was an aristocratic document, sealed by the great barons. But it expressed a powerful principle: a king who failed the nation could be rejected.

This is one of the major recurring themes in Scottish history. Monarchy mattered, but legitimacy was not unconditional. The political community could imagine itself as something prior to, and judge of, its king.

The Declaration also worked diplomatically. It was addressed to the Pope, who at the time was a major arbiter of European political legitimacy. By appealing to Rome with such a striking philosophical claim, the Scots embedded their independence in the wider European political order.

Stop and think
The Declaration of Arbroath has sometimes been read (anachronistically) as a precursor to documents like the American Declaration of Independence. Where does that comparison hold up, and where does it break down?
Quick check
True or False: The Declaration of Arbroath argued that the Scottish king's authority was unconditional and could not be revoked.
False. The Declaration argued the opposite: kingship was conditional. A king who failed the realm could be rejected by the community of the realm.
VII Late Medieval

Late Medieval Scotland and the Stewart Crown

After Bruce, Scotland remained independent, but independence did not mean stability. The late medieval kingdom was a dangerous place. Scottish kings had to manage powerful magnates, border warfare with England, Highland lordships, semi-independent islands, church politics, succession crises, and shifting foreign alliances.

The Auld Alliance with France became central. Scotland and France shared a common enemy in England, and this alliance shaped Scottish diplomacy, military culture, and elite identity for centuries.

The Stewart dynasty rose to prominence from 1371 onward. The spelling 'Stewart' is usually associated with the Scottish form; 'Stuart' became common through French influence, especially with Mary, Queen of Scots. By the 15th and early 16th centuries, Scotland was a kingdom with real institutions, but royal power was still contested. Kings could be energetic and ambitious, but they often faced violent nobles and dangerous international pressures.

Stop and think
The Auld Alliance shaped Scottish politics for centuries. What is gained, and what is lost, by tying a small country's foreign policy so tightly to a single great power?
Quick check
The 'Auld Alliance' was an alliance between Scotland and which country?
The Auld Alliance was a long-running Scottish–French alliance against their common enemy, England.
VIII James IV

James IV: Renaissance King and Catastrophic Gamble

James IV is one of Scotland's most compelling monarchs. He was charismatic, cultured, energetic, and politically capable. His court embraced Renaissance influences. He supported learning, naval power, diplomacy, and royal authority.

He also married Margaret Tudor, daughter of Henry VII of England, in 1503. This marriage later became extremely important because it created the dynastic link that allowed James VI of Scotland to inherit the English throne in 1603. The Union of the Crowns was made possible by this marriage.

But James IV made one fatal decision. Bound by the Auld Alliance, he invaded England in 1513 while Henry VIII was campaigning in France. The result was Flodden. At Flodden Field, James IV was killed, along with much of Scotland's nobility. It was a national trauma. Scotland did not merely lose a battle; it lost a king and a generation of elite leadership.

Flodden matters because it weakened Scotland at a crucial moment. It left the throne to a child, James V, and reopened the old nightmare of minority rule, factional struggle, and foreign pressure.

Stop and think
James IV is often celebrated for his accomplishments as a Renaissance king, but his reign ended in catastrophic defeat. How should historians weigh long-term cultural achievement against a single ruinous decision?
Quick check
James IV's 1503 marriage to Margaret Tudor mattered later because it...
Margaret Tudor was Henry VII's daughter. Her descendants, including her great-grandson James VI, inherited a strong claim to the English throne, which was realized in 1603.
IX James V

James V and the Storm to Come

James V, father of Mary, Queen of Scots, inherited a wounded kingdom. His reign was shaped by the need to control nobles, maintain independence from England, and preserve Scotland's Catholic identity during the rising Protestant Reformation.

He married into French Catholic power, first through Madeleine of Valois, then Mary of Guise. This reinforced Scotland's French connection and Catholic alignment.

James V's conflict with England ended disastrously at Solway Moss in 1542. Shortly afterward, he died. His only surviving legitimate child was a baby girl: Mary. Mary became queen when she was only days old.

That detail is crucial. Scotland was again ruled by an infant. And this time the child-queen was also a dynastic prize on the European stage. Henry VIII of England immediately recognized the opportunity and pressed for Mary to marry his son Edward, a campaign so coercive it became known to history as the 'Rough Wooing'.

Stop and think
How does ruling 'by an infant' actually work in practice? Who really holds power in such a situation, and what makes that period so dangerous?
Quick check
Fill in the blank: Mary, Queen of Scots, was born in 1542 to James V and his French second wife, ____ ____ ____.
Mary of Guise was a French Catholic noblewoman whose marriage to James V tied Scotland tightly to France and Catholicism just as the Reformation was beginning to bite.
X Mary I (Scotland)

Mary, Queen of Scots: The Child Queen

Mary, Queen of Scots was born into crisis at Linlithgow palace in 1542. She was not just a Scottish monarch. She was a European chess piece. Her claims and connections made her valuable and dangerous: Queen of Scotland by birth, Catholic in a kingdom moving toward Protestant reform, connected to the French royal house, and a potential claimant to the English throne through her great-grandmother Margaret Tudor.

England wanted influence over her. France wanted alliance through her. Scottish factions wanted control of her. Protestant reformers feared what she represented. Catholic powers saw her as hope.

As a child, Mary was sent to France, where she grew up in one of Europe's most sophisticated courts. She married the French dauphin, who became Francis II of France. For a brief moment, Mary was both Queen of Scots and Queen Consort of France.

Then Francis died young in 1560. Mary returned to Scotland in 1561 as a young widow. She came back to a kingdom transformed by the Reformation that had taken place in her absence.

Stop and think
Mary spent her formative years in France, not Scotland. How might that have shaped, and limited, her ability to read Scottish politics when she returned?
Quick check
Mary, Queen of Scots, briefly held which TWO crowns simultaneously?
Through her marriage to Francis II, Mary was Queen of Scots and Queen Consort of France until Francis's death in 1560.
XI Reformation

The Scottish Reformation

The Scottish Reformation was not merely a change in church services. It was a political revolution. The old Catholic Church had been tied to monarchy, aristocratic patronage, land, ritual, and European Catholic identity. Protestant reformers attacked not only doctrine but the entire structure of religious authority.

John Knox became the most famous reformer. He was severe, brilliant, uncompromising, and rhetorically ferocious. His Protestantism was Calvinist in shape: disciplined, scriptural, suspicious of images, hostile to Catholic worship, and wary of monarchy when monarchy threatened true religion.

In 1560, the Reformation Parliament abolished papal jurisdiction, banned the Mass, and adopted a Protestant confession of faith. Mary returned in 1561 as a Catholic queen to a country where Protestant nobles and ministers had gained enormous power. This created the central contradiction of her reign: she had legal legitimacy, but the Protestant movement had revolutionary momentum.

It is worth correcting one common impression. Mary did not immediately fail. She was politically intelligent, charming, and initially cautious. She tried to rule without provoking a full religious civil war. But her personal and dynastic decisions would prove politically explosive.

Stop and think
Knox famously detested the very idea of a female ruler. How might religious revolution and gender politics have reinforced each other in shaping the opposition to Mary?
Quick check
True or False: Mary, Queen of Scots, immediately attempted to reverse the Protestant Reformation upon her return to Scotland in 1561.
False. Mary was initially cautious and tried to rule without provoking religious civil war, though she maintained her own Catholic practice.
XII Reformation

Knox, the Kirk, and a Catholic Queen

The young Catholic queen and the Protestant preacher had several recorded encounters at Holyrood. These meetings have become almost legendary: the elegant French-raised monarch and the bearded prophet who refused to bow to the political consensus.

Knox represented something new in Scottish politics. The Kirk was not simply the king's church. Through structures of ministers, elders, assemblies, and synods, the Reformed church could organize itself independently of the crown. This was a radically new conception of religious authority.

For Mary, this was an impossible problem. Her legitimacy as queen was Catholic and dynastic. The country's emerging religious establishment was Protestant and increasingly distrustful of royal power over the church. A clever queen could navigate this in the short term. But the long-term tension would prove unmanageable, especially once Mary began to make personal decisions that handed her enemies powerful political weapons.

Stop and think
The relationship between Knox and Mary is often dramatized as a personal duel. How does focusing on personalities sometimes distort our understanding of large-scale political and religious change?
Quick check
What kind of Protestant theology did John Knox primarily promote?
Knox's theology was Calvinist, shaped heavily by his time in Geneva with John Calvin himself.
XIII Mary I (Scotland)

Mary and Darnley: Marriage as Disaster

Mary's marriage to Lord Darnley in 1565 was one of the most consequential mistakes of her life. Darnley was handsome, aristocratic, and had his own Tudor blood claim. On paper, he strengthened Mary's dynastic position. In reality, he was unstable, arrogant, and politically reckless.

Their marriage alarmed Elizabeth I of England because any child of Mary and Darnley would have an even stronger claim to the English succession.

At first, Darnley seemed like a useful match. Then he became a liability. The marriage collapsed into jealousy, factional politics, and violence. The most infamous episode was the murder of David Rizzio, Mary's Italian secretary, in 1566. Darnley and Protestant conspirators dragged Rizzio from Mary's presence and killed him.

The human angle is brutal. Mary was pregnant at the time. The murder was not only political intimidation. It was psychological warfare inside the queen's private chamber. Mary later gave birth to a son: James VI, the future king of both Scotland and England.

Stop and think
Why is the location of Rizzio's murder, inside Mary's private chamber, important to understanding the political meaning of the act?
Quick check
Who was David Rizzio?
Rizzio was Mary's Italian secretary. His murder in 1566 by Darnley and Protestant conspirators was as much an act of psychological terror against Mary as it was a political killing.
XIV Mary's Fall

The Murder of Darnley and the Bothwell Crisis

In 1567, Darnley was murdered after an explosion at Kirk o' Field. His body was found outside, suggesting he may have survived the blast and been killed afterward. Suspicion fell heavily on Earl of Bothwell. Then Mary married Bothwell.

This was politically catastrophic. Whether Mary was complicit in Darnley's murder remains one of the enduring controversies of Scottish history. Historians debate the evidence, including the so-called Casket Letters, whose authenticity and interpretation have long been contested.

But politically, perception mattered. By marrying Bothwell so soon after Darnley's murder, Mary made herself vulnerable to charges of scandal, complicity, and moral collapse.

Scottish nobles rebelled. Mary was imprisoned at Lochleven Castle and forced to abdicate in favor of her infant son, James VI, in 1567. She escaped in 1568, raised support, but was defeated at Langside near Glasgow. She fled to England, expecting aid from her cousin Elizabeth I. Instead, Elizabeth imprisoned her.

Stop and think
Whether Mary was actually complicit in Darnley's murder remains debated, but politically, perception destroyed her. What does that tell you about how political legitimacy operates?
Quick check
Which of the following is NOT true of the Bothwell crisis?
Elizabeth did not aid Mary. She imprisoned her, and Mary remained an English prisoner for nearly nineteen years.
XV Captivity

Mary in England: Prisoner, Symbol, Threat

Mary spent nearly nineteen years in English captivity. She was not kept in a dungeon the whole time; her imprisonment varied in comfort. But politically, she was trapped.

To English Catholics, Mary could be seen as the rightful queen. To Protestant England, she was a living threat. Every Catholic plot against Elizabeth made Mary more dangerous, whether or not she was actively directing it.

Eventually, Mary was implicated in the Babington Plot, a plan to assassinate Elizabeth and place Mary on the English throne. Elizabeth hesitated to execute an anointed queen, but the pressure became overwhelming. Mary was executed at Fotheringhay Castle in 1587.

This transformed her again: from failed queen to Catholic martyr, tragic heroine, and dynastic ghost haunting the Stuart future. Her son James did not go to war for her. That is one of the cold realities of dynastic politics. James protested, but not enough to endanger his own future claim to the English throne.

Stop and think
James VI did not fight to save his mother. Is that cold pragmatism, political wisdom, both, or something worse? How do you weigh family against the survival of a dynasty?
Quick check
Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed in which year, and at which castle?
Mary was executed in 1587 at Fotheringhay Castle, after being implicated in the Babington Plot against Elizabeth I.
XVI James VI

James VI: The Child King Who Learned Survival

James VI became king as an infant in 1567. His childhood was shaped by regents, factional violence, Protestant tutors, and the shadow of his mother's downfall. He learned early that kingship was performance, negotiation, and survival.

James grew up in a Scotland where royal authority was limited by powerful nobles and by the Kirk. The Protestant church did not want a king who behaved like a sacred absolute monarch. James, however, developed a strong theory of monarchy. He believed kings were appointed by God and should not be bullied by ministers or nobles.

This produced one of the great tensions of his reign. James wanted royal authority. The Scottish Kirk wanted religious independence. The nobility wanted influence. And England watched him closely as Elizabeth's likely successor.

James was not a warrior-king like Robert Bruce. He was a political operator. He survived by reading factions, delaying commitments, writing, arguing, and keeping his eyes on the English succession. His marriage to Anne of Denmark secured a Protestant northern alliance and produced a Protestant heir.

Stop and think
How is the kind of intelligence required to survive as a child king and outmaneuver factions different from the kind of intelligence required to lead an army to victory? Is one undervalued in popular history?
Quick check
James VI's approach to kingship is best described as:
James was a political operator first, intellectual second, and warrior almost never. His survival of regencies and factional violence is among the great underappreciated achievements of his career.
XVII James VI

James, Witchcraft, and the Kirk

James VI is also important for the history of witchcraft. He became personally interested in witch trials, especially after storms affected his voyage with Anne of Denmark from Denmark to Scotland. He believed witchcraft was real and dangerous.

His book Daemonologie in 1597 helped articulate elite demonological thinking. This did not create witch belief by itself, but it gave royal intellectual backing to persecution. Early modern Scotland was a deeply anxious society: religious conflict, poor harvests, local feuds, disease, political instability, and fear of Satanic conspiracy. Witchcraft accusations often emerged where theology, gender, social resentment, and fear collided.

James also understood something politically sharp about the Kirk. If the church could reject hierarchy, people might ask why the state needed hierarchy either. The phrase associated with him, ['No bishop, no king']](no bishop, no king), captured his view that church hierarchy helped support monarchy. A church without bishops, governed by independent Presbyterian assemblies, was structurally inconvenient for a king who wanted to control his realm.

James wanted bishops because bishops could be controlled more easily than independent assemblies. The struggle between king and Kirk would not end with him. It would explode under his son, Charles I, helping trigger the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.

Stop and think
James saw a structural link between church government and political government. Was he right that ecclesiastical hierarchies tend to reinforce political ones? Can you think of counterexamples?
Quick check
The phrase 'No bishop, no king' captures James VI's view that:
James believed structural hierarchy in the church reinforced structural hierarchy in the state. Get rid of bishops, and the logic that supports monarchy starts to look shaky too.
XVIII Union of the Crowns

The Union of the Crowns, 1603

In 1603, Elizabeth I of England died unmarried and childless. James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne as James I of England. This was the Union of the Crowns.

It did not create Great Britain as a single state. Scotland and England remained legally separate kingdoms with separate parliaments, churches, laws, and institutions. But they now shared one monarch.

This was one of the great ironies of Scottish history. For centuries, England had tried to dominate Scotland by war, diplomacy, marriage, and pressure. In 1603, a Scottish king inherited England.

But the triumph was ambiguous. James moved his court to London. Scotland gained prestige but lost the daily presence of its monarch. The Scottish political class now had to deal with a king whose attention was divided and increasingly centered on the richer, larger southern kingdom. James wanted a fuller political union. He liked the idea of 'Great Britain'. But English and Scottish elites were not ready for full parliamentary union in his lifetime. So 1603 created a dynastic union without institutional unity. That unresolved structure would produce instability throughout the 17th century.

Stop and think
Was 1603 a Scottish victory, an English victory, both, or something stranger that does not fit either category?
Quick check
The 1603 Union of the Crowns created:
The Union of the Crowns was dynastic only. Scotland and England remained legally separate. Full political union would not come until 1707.
XIX Synthesis

Why Mary and James Matter So Much

Mary and James are not just colorful figures. They sit at the hinge of Scottish history.

Mary represents the old Catholic, French-connected, dynastic Scotland. James represents the Protestant, British, union-minded future. Mary's life was shaped by medieval-style dynastic marriage politics. James's career points toward a composite monarchy ruling multiple kingdoms. Mary's tragedy belongs to the age of Reformation crisis. James's reign belongs to the birth of Britain as a political problem.

Their relationship is also strikingly cold in historical terms. Mary gave birth to the king who would inherit her claims, but James was raised by her enemies, ruled in her place, and ultimately benefited from the English succession that her existence had threatened. The mother died as a Catholic martyr. The son became the Protestant king of Scotland, England, and Ireland. That is the Stuart paradox.

By the early 1600s, Scotland had passed through several transformations: from tribal and regional societies into the Kingdom of Alba; from Gaelic kingship into a feudal medieval monarchy; from independence war into national mythology; from Catholic kingdom into Protestant Reformation state; from separate monarchy into dynastic union with England.

But the deepest tensions remained unresolved: Highland versus Lowland, Catholic versus Protestant, king versus Kirk, Scotland versus England, local lordship versus central authority, independence versus union. These tensions would define the next phase: the Covenanters, civil wars, Cromwell, Restoration, Jacobites, the 1707 Union, Culloden, the Highland Clearances, Enlightenment, empire, industrialization, and modern nationalism. That, however, is a story for Part 2.

Stop and think
Which of the unresolved tensions listed above strikes you as having the longest reach into modern Scottish identity and politics? Why?
Quick check
Which pair best captures the 'Stuart paradox' described in the section?
Mary died a Catholic martyr. Her son James VI became the Protestant king of Scotland, England, and Ireland, benefiting from the very succession her existence had threatened.
